title: Week 2, Lecture 3: More Formatting, Data Types, Errors, Order of Operations

lecture_blocks.title: Formatting with the format function, again

segments.text: ">" and "<" right and left justify, respectively. The format function returns a string which can be printed. It takes two arguments, the object to be formatted and the formatting string. The string returned is the length of the width of the field in the formatting string.
The "s" format specifier is for formatting strings. Here's an example that starts by formatting two strings of length five. I use a "ruler" which helps us see how things come out.

code_cells.content:
ruler="123456789-"
h="hello"
t="there"
# format takes two arguments, the object to be formatted and the formatting string
s1=format(h,"<10s") # returns a string of length 10
s2=format(t,">7s") # returns
print(s1)
print(s2)
# the len() function returns the length of a string
print(len(h),len(t),len(s1),len(s2))
# "\n" advances to the next line
print(ruler*2,"\n",s1,s2,sep="")

segments.text: Integers are formatted similarly to strings, but instead of the "s" format specifier, use the "d" format specifier, plus a width, as in the following example which prints out two integers, one with a width of 10 and another with a width of 7.

code_cells.content:
ruler="123456789-"
print(ruler*2,"\n",format(43213,"<10d"),
      format(12349,">7d"),sep='') # this is one way to continue a line

segments.text: Floating point numbers use the "f" format specifier. For instance, "10f.2" means the number should be formatted in a string of a total length of 10 with 2 places after the decimal point. The string is padded as needed on the left by spaces.

Note that format does not actually change the underlying floating point number it is formatting. This is done by the round function if desired. But it is not necessary to change a floating point number in order to show it rounded during printing by using the format function.
Here is an example.

code_cells.content:
a=1/6
print(a)
# ask the user for the two components of the format specifier
w=input("What width would you like?")
p=input("How many places after the decimal point?")
# construct the specifier from the numbers input
formatspec=w+"."+p+"f"
print(formatspec)
# format using the specifier
b=format(a,formatspec)
print(b)
b=format(a,"10.4f")
print(b)
# formatting doesn't change the underlying value
# note a is unchanged; this formatting does not round the variable a itself
print(a)
# to change the underlying value, use the round function
a=round(a,3) # this "round" function actually rounds the variable a
print(a)
print(round(a,1))
print(a)

segments.text: The "f" and "d" format specifiers allow for formatting numbers so that commas appear every three digits starting from the right of the number, as in the following example.

code_cells.content:
ruler="123456789-"
a=12345.5789
print(format(a,".3f")) # without comma separators
print(format(a,",.3f")) # with comma separators
print(format(a,",.0f")) # comma separators and rounding to nearest whole number
print(2*ruler)
# with comma separators, field width and justificaiton
print(format(a,">15,.1f"))
print(format(a,"<10,.2f"),format(a,">10,.1f"), sep="")
x=123455555555555555555929292933999129394995919293293932991233
print(x)
print(format(x,",d"))

segments.text: In addition, one of the other ways to control format through the use of "f-strings" (also known as "formatted string literals") which have become popular more recently. We won't cover these in detail, but the following are a couple of examples. You can use f-strings in your programs if you like. They are my favorite way to do formatting in Python because they are so concise compared to the other methods. They use the same format specifiers as the other methods.

segments.text: Here is an example:

code_cells.content:
# variables are included in the f-string in braces
# format is given after a colon in the braces
price=2.5
# version using an f-string
print(f'The price is ${price:.2f}')
# version using the format statement
print("The price is $",format(price,".2f"),sep="")
speed_of_light=186282.39705122
print(f'The speed of light is {speed_of_light:,.3f} miles per second.')

segments.text: Python stores different types of data as objects in the RAM (random access memory) of the computer.
Python supports many types of objects , but initially we will work with four types:

items: strings (e.g. "hello") (class 'str')
integers (e.g. 17, no decimal point) (class 'int')
floating point numbers (e.g. 5.2, decimal point) (class 'float')
boolean values (True or False) (class 'bool')

segments.text: Let's generate a random integer between 1 and 100 and then see if it is even or odd. Each time I run the program I will get a different number generated by the "random" module.

code_cells.content:
import random
my_random_number=random.randint(1,100)
s1="The random number is:"
print(s1, my_random_number)

s2="Is it even?"
if ((my_random_number%2)==0):
  even=True
else:
  even=False
print(s2,even)
print(type(even)) # the "type" function tells us the type of an object

segments.text: Python allows you to access the mathematical constant pi through the math module, as follows:

code_cells.content:
import math
pi=math.pi
print(pi)
print(type(pi))

lecture_blocks.title: Computing the Area and Perimeter of a Circle

segments.text: We can use pi to compute the area and perimeter of a circle given its radius, as in the following example:

code_cells.content:
import math
radius=float(input("Enter the radius of the circle:"))
perimeter=2*math.pi*radius
area=math.pi*(radius**2)
print("The perimeter of the circle is:", format(perimeter,"10.3f"))
print("The area of the circle is", format(area,"10.3f"))

# both of the new variables are floats
print(type(area))
print(type(perimeter))

segments.text: You can put commas or symbols inside numeric values. The following is not allowed:

code_cells.content:
x=$1,234
print(x)

segments.text: If a number has a decimal point in it, it is a float, even if it is a whole number.

code_cells.content:
x=6.0
print(type(x))
x=6
print(type(x))

segments.text: Which of these is not a float?

items: They are all floats

segments.text: The result of a division is always a float, even if both operands are integers, as in the following example:

code_cells.content:
x=12
print(type(x))
y=6
print(type(y))
z=x/y
print(z)
print(type(z))

segments.text: The result of integer division is an int.

code_cells.content:
x=13
y=6
z=x//y
print(z)
print(type(z))

segments.text: The result of an integer division rounds down from what it would be if you did a floating point division. This is true even for negative numbers.

code_cells.content:
print(5/2)
print(5//2)
print(-5/2)
print(-5//2)
print(11/3)
print(11//3)

lecture_blocks.title: Converting a String to an Int or a Float

segments.text: You can convert a string containing just numeric characters to an int or a float.
segments.html: You can convert a string containing just numeric characters to an int or a float.<br class="amber-el amber-break">

code_cells.content:
x="2"
print(type(x)) # string
x=int(x)
print(type(x)) # int
y="2.6"
print(type(y)) # string
y=float(y)
print(type(y)) # float

lecture_blocks.title: Python: Dynamically Typed, Not Statically Typed

items: You don't need to declare the type of data that your variables will hold (which you do need to do in many other languages)
In addition, the type of data held by a variable can change and is defined by what you put in it.
This is called "dynamic" typing" (as opposed to "static" typing)

segments.text: For example:

code_cells.content:
my_var="Hello"
print(my_var,type(my_var))
my_var=3.0
print(my_var,type(my_var))
my_var=3
print(my_var,type(my_var))

lecture_blocks.title: Dynamically and Statically Typed Computer Languages: Some Examples

items: Dynamically Typed: Python, PHP, JavaScript, Perl, Ruby
Statically Typed: C, C++, Java, Swift

segments.text: Here some code that defines three statically typed variables in Java.
String name = "Harry";int top_speed = 50;float gravity = 9.5;
String name = "Harry";int top_speed = 50;float gravity = 9.5;

Note that in Java, all variables need to be given a type before they are assigned a value, and the value assigned needs to match that type. You can't assign a floating point to a variable declared as a String, for instance.

lecture_blocks.title: Using the output of the "input" function in calculations

items: The input function always returns a string
This string cannot be used in numerical calculations
We therefore need to convert it to an int or float
We "wrap" the call to input() in a call to int() or float()

segments.text: An example:

code_cells.content:
score1=int(input("Enter the score of team #1:"))
score2=int(input("Enter the score of team #2:"))
print("The total score is:", score1+score2)

segments.text: Suppose the user has some American change: pennies (one cent), nickels (five cents), dimes (ten cents), and quarters (twenty-five cents). Write a program to ask the user how many coins he or she has of each type and then print out their total value.
As you write code, you are likely to encounter errors. These errors will be one of the following three types:

items: Syntax errors: your program isn't correct Python
Runtime errors: your program is correct Python, but something averse happens when you run it, like dividing by zero
Logic errors: your program is correct Python, and there aren't any runtime errors, but you made a logical error when you wrote your program

lecture_blocks.title: An Example of a Syntax Error

segments.text: The following is a syntax error, because the string delimiters don't match.

code_cells.content: print("hello world')

segments.text: The following code will generate a runtime error if you don't enter a number, because the conversion to float will fail.

code_cells.content:
num=float(input("Please enter a number:"))
print(num)

segments.text: The following code represents a logic error because you subtracted when you intended to add.

code_cells.content:
num1=float(input("Enter a number:"))
num2=float(input("Enter another number:"))
print("The sum is",num1-num2)

segments.text: Python uses the standard order of operations (PEMDAS)

items: Parentheses
Exponents
Multiplication/Division (left to right)
Addition/Subtraction (left to right)

segments.text: People use the pneumonic "please excuse my dear Aunt Sally" to remember this.
You can use parentheses to get any order you want.

   4*7)

segments.text: The "+" operator in the context of strings means concatenation, that is, adding one string to the end of another.

code_cells.content:
s1="hello"
s2="world"
s3=s1+" "+s2
print(s3)
print(len(s3))

segments.text: The "*" operator in the context of strings allows you to repeat a string.

code_cells.content:

print(y)
print(len(y))
